AI.conclusion: No single pipeline universally outperforms others. The contribution is a dataset-aware, compute-conscious decision framework rather than a universal superiority claim, guiding practitioners on when deep learning is worth its cost for sustainable healthcare analytics.

title: Coevolution of epidemic dynamics and network topology driven by disease fatality and waning immunity
summary: Epidemics on complex networks have been shown to exhibit dynamics that are strongly influenced by the topology of the network. However, it remains unclear how the topology of the network is influenced by epidemic properties, such as waning immunity and disease fatality, coupled with demographic changes. To explore the interplay between epidemic dynamics and network topology, we develop an agent-based model of a fatal infectious disease with an imperfect immunity on an initially scale-free network that evolves via demographic and epidemic-induced changes. We show that this model undergoes an epidemic transition between a phase in which the disease eventually dies out and a phase in which it becomes endemic. Moreover, the network may lose its scale-free property as a result of the epidemic spreading, giving rise to a topological transition from a power-law to a non-power-law degree distribution. We validate our findings using heterogeneous mean-field approximations of the agent-based model. These results highlight the importance of accounting for network evolution in epidemic models and advance our understanding of coevolving dynamical systems, in which disease dynamics and network topology continuously shape one another.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an agent-based model of a fatal infectious disease with imperfect immunity on an evolving scale-free network, showing both an epidemic transition (from extinction to endemic) and a topological transition (from power-law to non-power-law degree distribution) driven by epidemic-demographic feedback loops.
AI.motivation: While prior work has shown that network topology influences epidemic dynamics, it remains unclear how epidemic properties (waning immunity, disease fatality) coupled with demographic changes influence network topology in return.
AI.method: The authors develop an agent-based model of a fatal infectious disease with imperfect immunity on an initially scale-free network that evolves via demographic (birth/death) and epidemic-induced changes. They validate findings using heterogeneous mean-field approximations.
AI.result: The model exhibits an epidemic transition between disease extinction and endemic phases. Additionally, the network can lose its scale-free property due to epidemic spreading, resulting in a topological transition from a power-law to a non-power-law degree distribution.
AI.conclusion: These results highlight the importance of accounting for network evolution in epidemic models and advance understanding of coevolving dynamical systems where disease dynamics and network topology continuously shape one another.

title: AMPBench-MT: A Homology-Controlled Benchmark for Antimicrobial Peptide Potency, Spectrum, and Safety Prediction
summary: Computational AMP discovery is often evaluated through AMP/non-AMP recognition, yet follow-up decisions depend on assay-derived evidence such as target-species potency, hemolysis, toxicity, and selectivity. Existing AMP and peptide benchmarks cover binary recognition, multilabel annotation, assay regression, or broader peptide-model comparison, but they do not jointly place AMP recognition, species-conditioned potency, spectrum, safety-facing proxy endpoints, and cross-endpoint behavior within one sequence-homology-controlled protocol. To address this problem, we introduce AMPBench-MT, a provenance-preserving benchmark that standardizes canonical peptide records and organizes them into binary recognition, species-conditioned pMIC regression, and endpoint-specific potency and safety-facing readouts. Across 161 endpoint-specific model evaluations, high binary performance does not reliably indicate assay-endpoint behavior. Frozen protein-language-model embeddings form the leading pMIC error cluster, while graph and classical regressors remain close. Spectrum labels further reveal that PR-oriented metrics can be misleading under scarce observed negatives, whereas low-toxicity, HC50 hemolysis, and selectivity expose smaller but more assay-facing signals. AMPBench-MT shows that AMP evaluation should move beyond recognition leaderboards toward endpoint-aware evidence auditing. Our proposed benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ZihengZhou06/AMPBench-MT.

AI.tldr: AMPBench-MT is a new benchmark for antimicrobial peptide (AMP) discovery that goes beyond binary recognition to include species-conditioned potency, safety proxies (hemolysis, toxicity, selectivity), and cross-endpoint analysis. Results show high binary performance does not guarantee good assay-endpoint behavior, advocating for endpoint-aware evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing AMP benchmarks only cover binary recognition, multilabel annotation, or regression in isolation, without jointly evaluating recognition, species-conditioned potency, safety endpoints, and cross-endpoint behavior under a homology-controlled protocol. This gap leads to misleading follow-up decisions in real AMP discovery.
AI.method: The authors propose AMPBench-MT, a provenance-preserving benchmark that standardizes canonical peptide records and organizes them into: (1) binary recognition, (2) species-conditioned pMIC regression, and (3) endpoint-specific potency and safety-facing readouts. They evaluated 161 endpoint-specific model configurations.
AI.result: High binary recognition performance does not reliably indicate good assay-endpoint behavior. Frozen protein-language-model embeddings dominate pMIC regression errors; graph and classical regressors remain competitive. Spectrum labels show PR metrics can mislead under scarce negatives. Low-toxicity, HC50 hemolysis, and selectivity reveal smaller but more assay-facing signals.
AI.conclusion: AMP evaluation should move beyond recognition leaderboards toward endpoint-aware evidence auditing. The benchmark is publicly available on Hugging Face.

title: Global Dynamics of Trait-Structured Generalised Lotka-Volterra Systems with Trait-Independent Interactions
summary: We study the long time dynamics of a selection-mutation integro-differential Lotka-Volterra system of $N$ populations. In our model, fitness depends on a continuous phenotypic trait, but the effect of one population on another is independent of this trait. We establish that, under some usual assumptions on the interactions between populations, the long time behaviour of solutions is exactly determined by the well studied Generalised Lotka-Volterra (ordinary differential) Equation. We also show that, all else being equal, the minimal mutation rate is selected for in a static environment, whereas in an a changing environment, an intermediate mutation rate could be selected instead. The key step in our proofs is establishing that the total population sizes are asymptotically governed by a Generalised Lotka-Volterra Equation, which then allows the use of a general result on asymptotically autonomous dynamical systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that the long-term dynamics of a selection-mutation Lotka-Volterra system with continuous traits reduce to the classical Lotka-Volterra ODE, showing minimal mutation is favored in static environments while intermediate mutation can be selected in changing environments.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between complex integro-differential selection-mutation models and simpler ordinary differential equation (ODE) frameworks, and to understand how environmental stability affects mutation rate selection in population dynamics.
AI.method: The authors establish that total population sizes asymptotically follow a Generalized Lotka-Volterra Equation, then apply a general result on asymptotically autonomous dynamical systems to characterize long-term behavior.
AI.result: Under standard assumptions on inter-population interactions, the long-time solution behavior is exactly determined by the Generalized Lotka-Volterra ODE. Minimal mutation rate is selected in static environments, while intermediate mutation rates can be selected in changing environments.
AI.conclusion: The selection-mutation model can be reduced to a simpler ODE framework, with environment stability being a key factor in determining optimal mutation rates.

title: Contrastive Representation Learning of Longitudinal Disease Trajectories on Temporal Graphs
summary: Understanding disease trajectories from longitudinal clinical data remains challenging due to complex temporal dynamics and heterogeneous patient cohorts. Here, we present a contrastive representation learning framework that models multivariate disease trajectories as temporal graphs and learns representations using contrastive graph neural networks. Nodes represent patient observations over time, while edges capture temporal continuity and structural similarity between trajectories. Structure-aware random walks guide contrastive learning to generate embeddings that preserve temporal context and trajectory topology. The resulting representations enable robust clustering of patients with similar disease progression patterns and reveal latent structure in longitudinal data.

AI.tldr: A contrastive graph neural network framework that models disease trajectories as temporal graphs to learn representations for clustering patients with similar progression patterns.
AI.motivation: Understanding disease trajectories from longitudinal clinical data is challenging due to complex temporal dynamics and heterogeneous patient cohorts.
AI.method: Models multivariate disease trajectories as temporal graphs where nodes represent patient observations over time and edges capture temporal continuity and structural similarity. Uses structure-aware random walks to guide contrastive graph neural networks for learning embeddings that preserve temporal context and trajectory topology.
AI.result: The resulting representations enable robust clustering of patients with similar disease progression patterns and reveal latent structure in longitudinal data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed contrastive representation learning framework effectively addresses challenges in modeling disease trajectories and discovers meaningful patient subgroups from longitudinal clinical data.

title: GraphIDyOM: A graph-native Python reimplementation of IDyOM for musical expectation modelling
summary: The Information Dynamics of Music model (IDyOM) has played a central role in computational accounts of musical expectation by providing event-by-event estimates of uncertainty and surprise from symbolic musical sequences. However, its reference implementation is difficult to integrate with contemporary Python workflows, and its internal memory structures are not easily accessible for inspection or modification. We introduce GraphIDyOM, a graph-native Python reimplementation of IDyOM that represents long-term and short-term predictive memories as explicit graph objects while preserving the model's variable-order, multiple-viewpoint architecture. GraphIDyOM returns event-wise information content and entropy, exposes internal memory structures for analysis and export, and supports access through a local server. We validate the implementation against the original Lisp IDyOM across single, projected, and multiple-viewpoint configurations, and benchmark its coverage and computational performance against a recent reimplementation. We then demonstrate how the explicit memory representation supports network analysis of learned memories, projection of expectation values onto musical networks, recency-sensitive memory retrieval, and interactive applications. GraphIDyOM therefore provides both a faithful and accessible reimplementation of a widely used model and a platform for studying musical expectation through memory, topology, and interaction.

AI.tldr: GraphIDyOM is a Python reimplementation of the IDyOM musical expectation model that uses explicit graph structures for memory representation, validated against the original, enabling network analysis and interactive applications.
AI.motivation: The original IDyOM implementation is difficult to integrate with modern Python workflows and its internal memory structures are not easily accessible for inspection or modification.
AI.method: GraphIDyOM reimplements IDyOM using explicit graph objects for long-term and short-term predictive memories, preserving variable-order, multiple-viewpoint architecture, and exposes internal structures via a local server.
AI.result: Validated against original Lisp IDyOM across multiple configurations, benchmarked for coverage and performance, and demonstrated for network analysis, memory retrieval, and interactive applications.
AI.conclusion: GraphIDyOM provides a faithful and accessible reimplementation of IDyOM and a platform for studying musical expectation through memory, topology, and interaction.
